conceptTag: Adidas and Puma: two brothers split
readerTitle: Adidas and Puma: the perfect founding pair that split in two
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Dassler 형제, Adidas, Puma) + 전해지는 일화 (방공호 일화, '굽은 목의 마을') + 가상 적용 (자매가 운영하는 식당)
insight: 보완적인 역량은 회사를 세우지만 지켜 주지는 않는다. 의견이 갈릴 때 누가 정하는지, 갈라설 때 어떻게 나누는지 미리 합의해야 갈등이 감당할 만한 크기로 남는다.
misconception: 만드는 사람과 파는 사람처럼 역량이 잘 맞는 가족이나 친구라면 서면 합의는 필요 없다. 공동창업자가 갈라서면 사업은 끝난다.

sources.text: Barbara Smit, Sneaker Wars (2008; UK title Pitch Invasion): 형제의 역할 분담, 같은 집에서 산 두 가족, 전쟁기 의심, 1948년 분리, 마을의 분열, 방공호 일화
adidas Group 공식 회사 연혁 (Dassler 형제의 창업, Jesse Owens 1936, 1949년 adidas 등록)
PUMA 공식 회사 연혁 (1948년 Rudolf Dassler의 회사 설립, Ruda에서 Puma로 이름 변경)

factChecks.note: 창업 시기('1920년대'), Jesse Owens가 1936년 베를린 올림픽에서 Dassler 신발을 신고 금메달 4개를 딴 사실을 adidas 공식 연혁으로 다시 확인하세요.
분리 연도 1948년, Rudolf의 회사 이름이 Ruda를 거쳐 Puma가 된 과정, Adi의 회사가 1949년 adidas로 등록된 사실을 두 회사 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요.
Rudolf가 아우라흐 강 건너편에 회사를 세웠다는 내용, 직원들이 편을 나눴다는 내용, 마을 상점·술집·축구 클럽이 편을 갈랐다는 내용, '굽은 목의 마을' 별명은 Smit(2008)과 여러 언론 보도에 나옵니다. 세부는 일화성이 있어 카드에 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다.
방공호 일화(Adi가 연합군 폭격기를 욕한 말을 Rudolf가 자기 가족을 향한 말로 받아들였다는 이야기)는 일화로 표시했습니다. 출처마다 표현이 다릅니다.
형제의 지분 구조와 공식 합의 여부는 확인하지 않았습니다. 카드 4·5의 '합의된 결정 방식이 없었다'는 내용은 사실 주장이 아니라 해석으로 썼습니다('seem to have lacked'). 게시 전 표현을 다시 검토하세요.
'형제가 끝내 화해하지 않았다'는 내용은 널리 보도되었지만 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다. '분쟁이 새 경쟁자에게 틈을 주었다'는 일부 저자의 주장으로만 쓰고, 증명하기 어렵다고 밝혔습니다. 매출이나 시장점유율 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two brothers, one shoe company, and a town split by a river
body: In the 1920s, Adi and Rudolf Dassler began making sports shoes together in Herzogenaurach, a small town in Germany. Adi designed and built the shoes. Rudolf sold them.
In 1936, Jesse Owens wore their shoes as he won four gold medals at the Berlin Olympics. On paper they were the perfect founding pair. Then it fell apart, and the breakup created **Adidas and Puma**.

image.label: Two brothers back to back on either side of a small river, each holding a running shoe
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 강을 사이에 두고 1940년대 옷차림의 두 형제가 등을 맞대고 서 있고, 각자 손에 클래식 러닝화를 든 모습. 강 양쪽에 작은 공장 건물 하나씩. 실제 Adidas·Puma 로고, 삼선, 폼스트라이프는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's 1948. The brothers can't work together.
body: The business has survived the war, but the brothers barely speak. Their families have shared one house, and suspicion runs both ways. Each brother believes the company depends on him.
If you were advising them, what would you suggest?

options.text: Split the company: divide the factories and staff, and compete
options.feedback: Each brother gets full control quickly. The cost is two firms chasing the same customers from the same small town, with nothing to stop the fight from getting personal.

options.text: One brother buys the other out
options.feedback: You get one clear owner and no rival next door. But it needs a fair price and money to pay it, and the brother who leaves can still start again.

options.text: Stay together, write down who decides what, and bring in an outsider to break ties
options.feedback: This keeps their combined strengths. But rules only work if both partners still trust each other enough to follow them, and by 1948 that trust was mostly gone.

choice.afterReveal: They chose to split. In 1948 Rudolf left and started his own company, which became Puma. Adi's company became Adidas.

cards.title: One town, two companies.
body: Rudolf set up across the river Aurach and soon named his company Puma. Adi named his after himself: **Adi Das**sler became Adidas. Workers had to pick a side.

The town split too. Shops, pubs and football clubs were reportedly known as Adidas or Puma places. Herzogenaurach got the nickname "the town of bent necks", because people looked at your shoes before deciding how to talk to you.
The brothers reportedly never made peace.

image.label: A small town map divided by a river, buildings colored in two shades
image.brief: 위에서 내려다본 작은 마을 지도 일러스트. 가운데로 강이 흐르고, 강 왼쪽 건물(빵집, 술집, 축구장)은 한 색, 오른쪽은 다른 색. 거리의 작은 사람들이 서로의 신발을 내려다보는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고와 색 조합은 피함.

cards.title: Complementary skills build a company. They don't hold it together.
body: Founders who cover different jobs, like a maker and a seller, have a strong start. But skills don't answer the hard questions: **who decides when you disagree**, how credit and money are shared, and what happens if one of you wants out.
The Dasslers had the skills. What they seem to have lacked was an agreed way to disagree and an agreed way to part. Without those, every dispute had nowhere to go but personal.
cards.softwareNote: In a startup this is the founders' agreement: who has the final say on product versus sales, how shares vest, and what happens to a leaving founder's shares. It's easiest to write in month one, while everyone still gets along.

cards.title: Why a family argument became a split.
body: Accounts differ on the exact cause. One story, often told and possibly embellished: in a wartime air-raid shelter, Adi cursed the bombers overhead, and Rudolf thought he meant Rudolf's family. The common threads are more useful than any single story:
list: **Nothing was separate:** work, family and home were shared, so no conflict stayed small
**No referee:** nothing clear settled who had the final word
**Credit:** each brother believed the success was mostly his
**Outside stress:** wartime suspicion, reportedly including accusations against each other
cards.callout: Conflict was likely. A way to handle it was missing.

cards.title: The breakup didn't destroy the business. It split it, at a price.
body: Here's what makes this case unusual. Both companies grew into global brands. The split did not wipe out what the brothers had built.

But the cost was real: decades of rivalry in one small town, effort spent fighting each other, and a divided family. Some business writers argue the feud also left room for newer rivals, though that is hard to prove.
So the lesson isn't "never split". It's that **how you split decides how much it costs**.

cards.title: Paper doesn't create trust.
body: A written agreement would not have fixed a family feud made worse by a war. Agreements work when partners still mostly trust each other. They decide who wins a deadlock, not whether you respect each other.
Also, much of the Dassler story comes from later books and local memory. Treat the vivid details as stories, not court records.

cards.title: Now it's a family restaurant.
body: Two sisters run a busy restaurant. One is the chef. The other runs the front of house and the money. It works, but arguments are growing over menu prices, hiring and whether to open a second site. Nothing is written down.

options.text: Leave it. They're family, and business is good
options.feedback: This avoids an awkward talk now. But the hardest questions show up when things go badly, which is the worst time to answer them.

options.text: Agree in writing who decides what, how deadlocks get settled, and how one could buy the other out
options.feedback: It costs one uncomfortable evening. In return, future fights become following a rule, and either sister has a fair way out.

options.text: Give the final say on everything to whoever owns slightly more
options.feedback: It ends deadlocks fast, but the other sister may feel her own area isn't hers anymore. Splitting decisions by area usually fits better.

cards.softwareNote: Two app co-founders face the same choice. A CTO and a CEO who split decisions by area, and agree on vesting and buyouts early, can part without taking the product down with them.

cards.title: Agree how you'll disagree, and how you'd part, while you still like each other.
body: The Dasslers had an ideal mix of skills. What broke them was everything skills can't settle.
**Try it today:** write down three decisions you and a partner might disagree on. For each, note who has the final say. If you can't, that's your next conversation.
